Reproducing Senzai & Buzsaki (2017) from dandiset 000003¶

Paper. Senzai Y, Buzsaki G (2017). Physiological properties and behavioral correlates of hippocampal granule cells and mossy cells. Neuron 93:691-704. doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2016.12.011. This attempt used the full text of the accepted author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC5293146); the version of record is not open access, and the supplementary figures were not available.

Dandiset. DANDI:000003, version 0.260218.2052. The paper cites no DANDI version (it points to CRCNS). This is the most recent of four published versions (0.210812.1448, 0.230629.1955, 0.250624.0409, 0.260218.2052). All four hold the same 101 assets with the same paths, sizes and content checksums, and differ only in metadata (contributors, keywords, schema version), none of which the analysis uses; the data check prints the comparison.

What the dandiset holds. One NWB file per recording (101 files from 16 mice over 94 days; seven dates hold two files): sorted units with a cell type label, spike times and per-spike waveforms; sleep and wake periods; the LFP; type 2 dentate spike (DS2) events; light pulse times; and, on days with behaviour, positions on the circular T-maze and in the open fields, with the T-maze trials. The raw wide-band signal is in 17 files, where it is used to read each unit's site and unfiltered waveform.

Code read. The paper links no code. The dandiset was converted with the CatalystNeuro conversion code: buzsaki_lab_to_nwb/yuta_mossy_cell in https://github.com/catalystneuro/buzsaki-lab-to-nwb at commit 5f6a3750 (current), and the earlier script original_code/convert_yuta.py at commit e4652c1 (February 2020), which matches the file format. They show where the labels come from: cell_type maps the authors' fineCellType codes (1 is a GC in the dentate and a CA3 pyramidal cell in CA3), and missing marks units with no row in the authors' unit summary. The T-maze positions are the authors' twhl_linearized and twhl_norm, scaled by 0.325 m and 0.46 m. The monosynaptic connections the authors detected (MonoSynConvClick.mat) were not converted.

No outside data are used. Random draws use a generator seeded in their own section.

The 16 subjects match the paper's 16 mice, but the genotypes do not: the files give 6 SST-Cre, 5 Drd2-Cre::Ai35, 4 POMC-Cre::Arch and 1 POMC-Cre::Ai35, against the paper's 7 SST-Cre, 5 DRD2-Cre::Ai35, 3 POMC-Cre::Ai35 and 1 wild type. Ai35 expresses Arch, so POMC-Cre::Arch and POMC-Cre::Ai35 may name the same cross; even so, the counts of SST-Cre, POMC and wild-type mice differ. Eighteen files have an older layout of the units table, with an electrode_group column that names each unit's shank; 17 of them also hold the waveforms. The other 83 files do not say which shank a unit was recorded on.

The labels follow the conversion code's mapping of the authors' codes. missing (237 units) marks units of the spike sorting with no row in the authors' summary, and unknown (1104) units the authors left unclassified. The interneuron labels do not say whether a unit is in the dentate gyrus or CA3; only label 1 was split by region (GC or CA3 pyramidal cell). Each unit has its own global_id, unique across files, so a unit is never the same across days; the probe was moved 70 um after each day (Methods), and units are counted once per day.

Largest distance of a spike time from the 20 kHz sample grid (samples): 1.1920928955078125e-07

In 24 files the second unit's stored spike train starts with a block of exactly 65,536 x k spikes (k = 1 to 7) that continues the first unit's train (the first such spike follows the first unit's last stored spike by 2 ms to 0.5 s) and then restarts at the beginning of the recording. The first unit's end index is short by a multiple of 2^16, as from an integer overflow at conversion. The loader gives these blocks back to the first unit; after that every unit's spike times increase. The same correction applies to the waveforms, which follow the spike order. A first unit whose true count exceeds the stored one but whose moved block does not break the order of the second unit's train cannot be detected this way. Spike times lie on the 20 kHz sample grid.

def overlaps(g):
    g = g.sort_values("start_time")
    return int((g.start_time.values[1:] < g.stop_time.values[:-1] - 1e-3).sum())
print("Overlapping periods within a file:", sum(overlaps(g) for _, g in st_all.groupby("session")))

# Clock check: rates of GC and CA3 units in NREM against awake periods, with the true labels and with
# the labels shifted by 30 min. If the states share the spike clock, the contrast should shrink.
def nrem_awake_contrast(shift):
    out = []
    for s in S:
        st = s["states"].copy()
        st[["start_time", "stop_time"]] += shift
        a, n = st[st.label == "awake"], st[st.label == "nrem"]
        da, dn = (a.stop_time - a.start_time).sum(), (n.stop_time - n.start_time).sum()
        if da < 300 or dn < 300:
            continue
        for u in s["units"][s["units"].type.isin(["GC", "CA3"])].unit:
            t = dg.times(s, u)
            ra = dg.interval_mask_count(t, a.start_time, a.stop_time) / da
            rn = dg.interval_mask_count(t, n.start_time, n.stop_time) / dn
            if ra > 0 and rn > 0:
                out.append(np.log2(rn / ra))
    return np.median(out), len(out)
for shift in (0, 1800, -1800):
    m, n = nrem_awake_contrast(shift)
    print(f"labels shifted by {shift:+5d} s: median log2(NREM rate / awake rate) of GC and CA3 units = {m:.2f} (n = {n})")

The states table holds awake, quiet, nrem, rem and transit periods; the paper names wake, NREM and REM. quiet is read as quiet wake, so wake is tested both as awake alone and as awake with quiet. The NREM against awake contrast of GC and CA3 rates is large with the true labels and much smaller with the labels shifted by 30 minutes, which is consistent with the states sharing the clock of the spikes.

The open-field positions span 0 to 1 and, scaled by the stored conversion of 0.46 m, cover the 46 cm arena of the Methods. The T-maze positions are documented only by their series names. The values show that column 0 runs along the central arm (0 to 2, so 65 cm at 0.325 m per unit) and column 1 is the angle along the circular side arms (pi radians at a 32.5 cm radius is 102 cm). This matches the maze in the Methods (central arm 65 cm, side arms 102 cm), so the reading is consistent with the data, but the files do not state it. Negative angles are the left arm: 98% of runs reach the arm that the trial's condition names. Both arm ends lie at the waiting area, and runs end 10 cm before the reward port (84 cm). Position samples are 25.6 ms apart (39 Hz), as the Methods say.

# Clock check for positions: spatial information of MC and CA3 units on the T-maze with true positions,
# and with the spike train shifted by 20 s (circularly within the session).
def info_with_shift(shift):
    vals = []
    for s in TM:
        units = s["units"][s["units"].type.isin(["MC", "CA3"])].unit.tolist()
        if not units:
            continue
        saved = {u: s["spikes"][u] for u in units}
        span = int((s["spike_time_range"][1] - s["spike_time_range"][0]) * dg.SPIKE_HZ)
        for u in units:
            s["spikes"][u] = np.sort((saved[u] + int(shift * dg.SPIKE_HZ)) % span).astype(np.int32)
        occ, maps, _ = dg.tmaze_maps(s, units)
        for u in units:
            vals.append(dg.spatial_info(np.concatenate(maps[u]), np.concatenate(occ)))
        s["spikes"].update(saved)
    return np.nanmedian(vals), len(vals)
for shift in (0, 20):
    m, n = info_with_shift(shift)
    print(f"spikes shifted by {shift:2d} s: median spatial information of MC and CA3 units = {m:.3f} bits/s (n = {n})")

# Recordings deposited twice: sessions of one mouse on the same date (the 'b' files) against each other.
from itertools import combinations
def coincidence(a, b, tol=0.0005):
    j = np.clip(np.searchsorted(b, a), 1, len(b) - 1)
    return float((np.minimum(np.abs(b[j] - a), np.abs(b[j - 1] - a)) < tol).mean())
by_day = {}
for s in S:
    by_day.setdefault((s["subject"], s["session"][-6:]), []).append(s)
rows = []
for (subj, day), group in by_day.items():
    for s1, s2 in combinations(group, 2):
        best = 0.0
        for u in s1["spikes"]:
            a = dg.times(s1, u)[:20000]
            for v in s2["spikes"]:
                b = dg.times(s2, v)
                if len(a) > 100 and len(b) > 100:
                    best = max(best, coincidence(a, b))
        n1, n2 = len(s1["positions"]), len(s2["positions"])
        rows.append({"pair": f"{s1['session']} / {s2['session']}", "units": f"{len(s1['spikes'])} / {len(s2['spikes'])}",
                     "max_coincident_spike_fraction": round(best, 3),
                     "same_states": s1["states"][["start_time", "stop_time"]].round(0).equals(s2["states"][["start_time", "stop_time"]].round(0)),
                     "same_unit_count": len(s1["units_all"]) == len(s2["units_all"])})
dups = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(dups.to_string(index=False))

        sig.setdefault(key, []).append(s["session"])

In the 17 files that give each unit's shank, the electrodes table numbers the sites of each shank 0 to 7 and gives no coordinates. The LFP and the wide-band signal have one column per electrode row, in table order, and their columns hold the same electrodes: the decimated wide-band signal of each column correlates best with the LFP column of the same index (printed above). The table's map does not fit the data. If the site numbers followed depth, the DS2 amplitude would change smoothly along them and cross zero once; it crosses more than once on 43 of the 64 shanks where it crosses at all. A unit's spike is largest in the wide-band signal on the shank the units table gives for only 45% of units, and on the table's own site for 9%. The stored waveforms are about 5 times larger than the same spikes in the wide-band signal (median 421 against 81 uV). The analysis therefore reads each unit's site from the wide-band signal, where the spike is largest, and takes the DS2 amplitude at that LFP column; the table's site is shown as a variant. The theta-reference channel has a positive DS2 in every one of these files, so it lies below the DS2 reversal.

# Which side of the mismatch is wrong? Each unit's shank (`electrode_group`) and the channel of its
# stored waveform where the spike is largest are paired with the wide-band column where its spike is
# largest. If the shanks and stored channels are right, each (shank, channel) should point to one
# column, the same in every file of the 4 mice (one probe layout). The map is built from the other
# mice and tested on each mouse in turn.
VOT = pd.DataFrame([{"session": s["session"], "subject": s["subject"], "unit": u, "shank": s["unit_site"]["units"][u]["shank"],
                     "channel": s["unit_site"]["units"][u]["channel"], "col": v["site_col"], "table_col": s["unit_site"]["units"][u]["col"]}
                    for s in SITE for u, v in s["raw_units"]["units"].items() if u in s["unit_site"]["units"] and v["n"] >= 20])
def vote_map(d):
    return d.groupby(["shank", "channel"]).col.agg(lambda c: c.value_counts().index[0])
CMAP = vote_map(VOT)
rng_map = np.random.default_rng(20170301)
held = []
for subj in sorted(VOT.subject.unique()):
    train, test = VOT[VOT.subject != subj], VOT[VOT.subject == subj]
    m = vote_map(train)
    perm = train.copy()
    for sess, idx in perm.groupby("session").groups.items():
        perm.loc[idx, ["shank", "channel"]] = perm.loc[idx, ["shank", "channel"]].values[rng_map.permutation(len(idx))]
    mp_ = vote_map(perm)
    key = list(zip(test.shank, test.channel))
    held.append({"subject": subj, "units": len(test),
                 "map_from_other_mice": np.mean([m.get(k, -1) == c for k, c in zip(key, test.col)]),
                 "same_with_units_shuffled": np.mean([mp_.get(k, -1) == c for k, c in zip(key, test.col)]),
                 "electrodes_table": float((test.table_col == test.col).mean())})
held = pd.DataFrame(held)
print(f"Units with at least 20 wide-band spikes: {len(VOT)}; (shank, stored channel) pairs seen: {len(CMAP)}, "
      f"pointing to {CMAP.nunique()} distinct columns")
print(f"Units whose wide-band column is the one their (shank, channel) points to, map from all mice: {(VOT.col.values == CMAP.loc[list(zip(VOT.shank, VOT.channel))].values).mean():.2f}")
print("Map from the other mice, tested on each mouse, against the same map with shanks and channels shuffled among units within each file, and the electrodes table:")
print(held.round(2).to_string(index=False))
el0 = SITE[0]["electrodes"]
print(f"\nRecovered map (stored channel 0 to 7 -> wide-band column; the shank of that column in the table of {SITE[0]['session']}):")
for sh in sorted(CMAP.index.get_level_values(0).unique()):
    cols = [int(CMAP.get((sh, ch), -1)) for ch in range(8)]
    print(f"  {sh}: {cols}  table: {[el0.group_name[c] if c >= 0 else '-' for c in cols]}")

# DS2 amplitude along the stored channel order of the recovered map, against the table's site numbers
# (the profiles of the data check above).
prof2 = []
for s in SITE:
    amp = 1e6 * s["unit_site"]["channel_amp"]
    for sh in sorted(CMAP.index.get_level_values(0).unique()):
        cols = [int(CMAP[(sh, ch)]) for ch in range(8) if (sh, ch) in CMAP.index]
        a = amp[cols]
        prof2.append({"session": s["session"], "shank": sh, "sites": len(a), "rho": stats.spearmanr(np.arange(len(a)), a)[0],
                      "sign_changes": int(np.sum(np.diff(np.sign(a)) != 0))})
prof2 = pd.DataFrame(prof2)
for name, d in (("recovered stored-channel order", prof2), ("table's site numbers", prof)):
    print(f"DS2 along the {name}: {len(d)} shanks, |Spearman rho| median {d.rho.abs().median():.2f}, >= 0.8 on {int((d.rho.abs() >= 0.8).sum())}; "
          f"crossing zero once on {int((d.sign_changes == 1).sum())} and more than once on {int((d.sign_changes > 1).sum())} of {int((d.sign_changes > 0).sum())} shanks that cross")

# The stored waveforms against the wide-band spike at the unit's site: which filtering of the
# wide-band mean they match, and their scale. Units with at least 100 wide-band spikes; the stored
# 32 samples are aligned to the 72-sample wide-band mean at the offset of best correlation.
wf = []
for s in SITE:
    conv = s["raw_units"]["conversion"]
    for u, v in s["raw_units"]["units"].items():
        if u not in s["waveforms"] or v["n"] < 100:
            continue
        w = s["waveforms"][u]
        st = w[int(np.argmax(np.ptp(w, axis=1)))].astype(float)
        versions = {"unfiltered": v["wave"].astype(float), "300 Hz": v["wave_hp"].astype(float)}
        for hz in (500, 800):
            versions[f"{hz} Hz"] = signal.filtfilt(*signal.butter(3, hz / (dg.SPIKE_HZ / 2), btype="high"), v["wave"].astype(float), padtype="even")
        r = {"session": s["session"], "unit": u, "conv_uV": 1e6 * conv}
        for name, x in versions.items():
            fits = []
            for o in range(len(x) - len(st) + 1):
                seg = x[o:o + len(st)] - x[o:o + len(st)].mean()
                fits.append((np.corrcoef(seg, st)[0, 1], o, np.dot(seg, st - st.mean()) / np.dot(seg, seg)))
            c, o, g = max(fits)
            r[f"r {name}"], r[f"offset {name}"], r[f"gain {name}"] = c, o, g
        wf.append(r)
WF = pd.DataFrame(wf)
print(f"\nStored against wide-band waveforms: {len(WF)} units with at least 100 wide-band spikes")
for name in ("unfiltered", "300 Hz", "500 Hz", "800 Hz"):
    print(f"  wide-band {name:>10}: correlation median {WF[f'r {name}'].median():.3f}; offset (samples) median {WF[f'offset {name}'].median():.0f}; "
          f"gain median {WF[f'gain {name}'].median():.2f} (IQR {WF[f'gain {name}'].quantile(0.25):.2f} to {WF[f'gain {name}'].quantile(0.75):.2f})")
print("Best-matching filtering per unit:", WF[[f"r {n}" for n in ("unfiltered", "300 Hz", "500 Hz", "800 Hz")]].idxmax(axis=1).str[2:].value_counts().to_dict())
print(f"Wide-band conversion factor: {WF.conv_uV.unique()} uV per count; its inverse {1 / WF.conv_uV.median():.2f}")

The units' shanks (electrode_group) and stored waveform channels are consistent with the wide-band signal, and the electrodes table is not. Each pair of shank and stored channel points to one wide-band column, the same across files and mice: a map built from the other three mice gives the column of a unit's largest spike for 78% to 89% of units in the fourth, against 0% to 9% with the shanks and channels shuffled among units and 5% to 13% with the electrodes table. The 63 pairs seen point to 63 distinct columns. Under this map each shank's 8 columns are not the table's block of 8 (shanks 3 and 4, and 5 and 6, share two table blocks), and the shank names differ (shank 1 of the units is the table's block 5). Along the stored channel order of this map the DS2 profile changes smoothly (median |rho| 0.88, against 0.35 along the table's site numbers) and crosses zero once on 43 of the 51 shanks that cross, so the stored channel order is consistent with depth. This supports the use of electrode_group in the variants that split units by shank, and the site read from the wide-band signal in mc-deeper and gc-mc-classification.

The stored waveforms match the wide-band spike at the unit's site best after a 300 Hz high-pass (median correlation 0.987, against 0.981 unfiltered and 0.867 at 800 Hz), with the trough aligned. Their gain over that signal (median 5.08) is close to the inverse of the wide-band conversion factor (1 / 0.195 uV per count = 5.13), which is consistent with waveforms stored in ADC counts and read as microvolts. Neither the filtering nor the scale is described in the files.

Unit measures¶

Rates by state, burst index, trough-to-peak latency, phase statistics and the DS2 response of every kept unit, used by several claims below.

In [15]:
started = time.time()
rows = []
for s in S:
    if not s["spikes"]:
        continue
    r = dg.state_rates(s)
    ut = s["units"].set_index("unit")
    r["type"] = [ut.type[u] for u in r.unit]
    r["bi"] = [dg.burst_index(dg.times(s, u)) for u in r.unit]
    tp = [dg.trough_to_peak_ms(s["waveforms"][u]) if u in s["waveforms"] else (np.nan, False, None) for u in r.unit]
    r["tp"] = [x[0] for x in tp]
    r["tp_at_end"] = [x[1] for x in tp]
    r["trough_ms"] = [np.argmin(x[2]) / 100.0 if x[2] is not None and np.isfinite(x[0]) else np.nan for x in tp]
    ru = s["raw_units"]["units"] if s["raw_units"] else {}
    raw = [(dg.trough_to_peak_ms(ru[u]["wave"][None])[:2] + dg.trough_to_peak_ms(ru[u]["wave_hp"][None])[:2]
            + (ru[u]["n"], ru[u]["site_col"], 1e6 * s["unit_site"]["channel_amp"][ru[u]["site_col"]]))
           if u in ru else (np.nan, False, np.nan, False, 0, -1, np.nan) for u in r.unit]
    for k, name in enumerate(("tp_raw", "tp_raw_at_end", "tp_rawhp", "tp_rawhp_at_end", "raw_n", "raw_col", "ds2_rawsite_uV")):
        r[name] = [x[k] for x in raw]
    for band in ("theta", "gamma"):
        st = [dg.phase_stats(s["phases"]["units"][u][band]) if s["phases"] else dg.phase_stats(np.array([])) for u in r.unit]
        for k in ("n", "mrl", "phase", "p", "kappa"):
            r[f"{band}_{k}"] = [x[k] for x in st]
    if len(s["ds2"]):
        d = [dg.ds2_response(dg.times(s, u), s["ds2"]) for u in r.unit]
        for k in ("peak_ratio", "peak_ms", "base_hz"):
            r[f"ds2_{k}"] = [x[k] for x in d]
    r["session"], r["subject"], r["genotype"] = s["session"], s["subject"], s["genotype"]
    rows.append(r)
R = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
for band in ("theta", "gamma"):
    R[f"{band}_sig"] = (R[f"{band}_p"] < 0.05) & (R[f"{band}_kappa"] > 0.1)
site = pd.DataFrame([{"session": s["session"], "unit": u, "ds2_site_uV": 1e6 * v["ds2_amp"], "shank": v["shank"], "site_channel": v["channel"], "table_col": v["col"]}
                     for s in S if s["unit_site"] for u, v in s["unit_site"]["units"].items()])
site["dentate_shank"] = [not (U[(U.session == a) & (U.electrode_group == b)].type == "CA3").any()
                         and (U[(U.session == a) & (U.electrode_group == b)].type.isin(["GC", "MC"])).any()
                         for a, b in zip(site.session, site.shank)]
R = R.merge(site, on=["session", "unit"], how="left")
print(f"{len(R)} units measured in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")
print(R.groupby("type")[["rate_overall", "rate_awake", "rate_quiet", "rate_nrem", "rate_rem", "bi", "tp"]].median().round(3).to_string())
print("\nDS2 measures missing (no events, or no spikes in the baseline):", R.ds2_peak_ratio.isna().groupby(R.type).sum().to_dict())
print("\nAwake time in the home cage (outside behaviour epochs and position series): %.0f of %.0f h" % (
    R.drop_duplicates("session").dur_awake_home.sum() / 3600, R.drop_duplicates("session").dur_awake.sum() / 3600))
print("Units with a wide-band waveform (at least 20 spikes):", (R.raw_n >= 20).groupby(R.type).sum().to_dict())

first-stage-labels¶

Narrow-waveform interneurons have a trough-to-peak latency below 0.425 ms, and among wide-waveform units the excitatory cells have a burst index above the threshold separating them from wide-waveform interneurons.

Result: partially reproduced. Under either burst threshold, 98.2% of GC and MC are wide-waveform and bursty, and 91.7% (threshold 1.2) or 93.3% (1.8) of wide-waveform interneurons are wide and not bursty, but only 82.5% of narrow-waveform interneurons have a trough-to-peak latency below 0.425 ms (from 40% to 100% by mouse). The labels pool dentate and CA3 interneurons: 92.7% of them are below 0.525 ms, the paper's CA3 threshold, and in the 17 files that give the shank, 94.4% of the 71 narrow-waveform interneurons on shanks with GC or MC and no CA3 unit are below 0.425 ms. The stored waveforms have their trough at 0.80 ms of 1.6 ms, so no latency above about 0.75 ms can be measured; the peak falls at the end for 43% of GC, 67% of MC, 16% of wide-waveform and 2% of narrow-waveform interneurons. On the wide-band signal of the 17 files (window to 2.4 ms after the spike), 64.7% of narrow-waveform interneurons are below 0.425 ms unfiltered, as the Methods measure it, and 88.5% after a 300 Hz high-pass.

interneuron-rates¶

Narrow-waveform interneurons fire faster than wide-waveform interneurons (medians 7.97 and 2.11 Hz; Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.00001).

Result: partially reproduced. Narrow-waveform interneurons fire faster than wide-waveform ones (Kruskal-Wallis P = 5.3e-17 over the recording, 1.4e-15 in awake periods), but the medians (5.96 and 2.57 Hz over the recording; 8.75 and 3.08 Hz awake) are outside the tolerance of 7.97 and 2.11 Hz under both readings. The labels include CA3 interneurons, which the paper counts apart. In the 17 files that give the shank, interneurons on shanks with GC or MC and no CA3 unit have medians of 8.56 and 2.29 Hz over the recording, both within tolerance (P = 3.7e-08); this variant does not decide the outcome.

Result: reproduced. The GC median trough-to-peak latency (0.710 ms) is below the MC median (0.740 ms; Mann-Whitney P = 2.3e-14). The result rests on units whose peak falls at the end of the stored 1.6 ms (43% of GC, 67% of MC), so it partly measures how often each type is cut off: among units with the peak inside the window, GC are not narrower (0.660 against 0.645 ms, P = 0.057). On the wide-band signal of the 17 files, where the window runs to 2.4 ms and few peaks reach its end (4% of GC, 9% of MC), the unfiltered waveform the Methods use gives GC 0.755 against MC 0.840 ms (P = 0.017); after a 300 Hz high-pass the two do not differ (0.710 against 0.720 ms, P = 0.4).

optotag-drd2¶

In DRD2-Cre::Ai35 mice, 29 of 107 putative mossy cells were suppressed by green light, against none of 202 putative granule cells, 8 of 68 wide-waveform and none of 69 narrow-waveform interneurons.

In [20]:
rows = []
for s in S:
    if "Drd2" not in s["genotype"] or len(s["pulse20"]) == 0:
        continue
    ut = s["units"].set_index("unit")
    for u in s["spikes"]:
        t = dg.times(s, u)
        a = dg.opto_response(t, s["pulse20"])
        b = dg.opto_response(t, s["pulse20"], base=(0.050, 0.200))
        rows.append({"session": s["session"], "subject": s["subject"], "type": ut.type[u],
                     "change_pre": a["change"], "p_pre": a["p_decrease"], "change_cycle": b["change"], "base_hz": a["base_hz"]})
O = pd.DataFrame(rows)
O["supp_pre"] = O.change_pre <= -dg.OPTO_DROP
O["supp_cycle"] = O.change_cycle <= -dg.OPTO_DROP

Result: partially reproduced. In the 26 DRD2-Cre::Ai35 sessions with 20 ms pulses (4 mice), the light suppresses MC far more often than GC, but at a much higher rate than the paper reports: 68 of 106 MC (0.642) with the baseline before the pulse and 71 (0.670) with the baseline later in the cycle, against 6 (0.030) and 13 (0.066) of 198 GC; the paper gives 29 of 107 MC and none of 202 GC. Adding a one-sided Poisson test (P < 0.05) to the 20% rule keeps all 68 MC and 5 GC. Wide-waveform interneurons are suppressed in 20 of 88 (paper 8 of 68) and narrow-waveform ones in 14 of 132 (paper 0 of 69). With a 50% threshold the MC fraction falls to 0.066, so the fraction depends strongly on a threshold the paper states as 20%. The 37 units of the Figure 1H legend equal the 29 MC and 8 wide-waveform interneurons of the text.

gc-nrem-highest¶

Granule cells fire most during NREM sleep and at similar rates during wake and REM.

In [22]:
def three_states(ty, wake_col):
    x = R[R.type == ty]
    groups = {"wake": x[wake_col].dropna(), "nrem": x.rate_nrem.dropna(), "rem": x.rate_rem.dropna()}
    kw = stats.kruskal(*groups.values()).pvalue
    post = {f"{a}-{b}": min(1.0, 3 * stats.mannwhitneyu(groups[a], groups[b]).pvalue) for a, b in (("nrem", "wake"), ("nrem", "rem"), ("wake", "rem"))}
    med = {k: round(v.median(), 3) for k, v in groups.items()}
    return med, kw, post
for wake_col, name in (("rate_awake", "(a) awake"), ("rate_wake_all", "(b) awake + quiet"), ("rate_awake_home", "variant, home-cage awake")):
    med, kw, post = three_states("GC", wake_col)
    print(f"GC, wake {name}: medians {med}; Kruskal-Wallis P = {kw:.2g}; Bonferroni-adjusted Mann-Whitney P: " + ", ".join(f"{k} {v:.2g}" for k, v in post.items()))
x = R[R.type == "GC"]
print("\nPaired view: GC with NREM above awake: %.2f; with NREM above REM: %.2f (n = %d)" % (
    (x.rate_nrem > x.rate_awake).mean(), (x.rate_nrem > x.rate_rem).mean(), len(x)))
print("By subject (GC medians, Hz):")
print(x.groupby("subject")[["rate_awake", "rate_quiet", "rate_nrem", "rate_rem"]].median().round(3).to_string())

theta-modulation¶

Granule cells are more strongly phase-modulated by theta oscillations than mossy cells and fire at later theta phases (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for both).

In [25]:
def circ_mean_deg(v):
    return float(np.degrees(np.angle(np.exp(1j * v).mean())))

def phase_claim(band):
    x = R[R.type.isin(["GC", "MC"])]
    print(f"Units with a {band} estimate: " + ", ".join(f"{t} {int((x[x.type == t][f'{band}_n'] >= 10).sum())}" for t in ("GC", "MC")))
    print(f"Modulated (Rayleigh P < 0.05, kappa > 0.1): " + ", ".join(f"{t} {int(x[x.type == t][f'{band}_sig'].sum())}" for t in ("GC", "MC")))
    sig = x[x[f"{band}_sig"]]
    g, m = sig[sig.type == "GC"], sig[sig.type == "MC"]
    print(f"MRL of modulated units: GC median {g[f'{band}_mrl'].median():.3f}, MC median {m[f'{band}_mrl'].median():.3f}, "
          f"Kruskal-Wallis P = {stats.kruskal(g[f'{band}_mrl'], m[f'{band}_mrl']).pvalue:.2g}")
    allg, allm = x[(x.type == 'GC') & x[f'{band}_mrl'].notna()], x[(x.type == 'MC') & x[f'{band}_mrl'].notna()]
    print(f"Variant, all units with an estimate: GC median MRL {allg[f'{band}_mrl'].median():.3f}, MC {allm[f'{band}_mrl'].median():.3f}, "
          f"P = {stats.kruskal(allg[f'{band}_mrl'], allm[f'{band}_mrl']).pvalue:.2g}")
    print(f"Spikes per modulated unit: GC median {g[f'{band}_n'].median():.0f}, MC median {m[f'{band}_n'].median():.0f} "
          "(the MRL of a uniform phase with n spikes is about 0.89 / sqrt(n))")
    print(f"Variant, MRL above the uniform-phase expectation 0.89/sqrt(n): GC median {(g[f'{band}_mrl'] - 0.89 / np.sqrt(g[f'{band}_n'])).median():.3f}, "
          f"MC {(m[f'{band}_mrl'] - 0.89 / np.sqrt(m[f'{band}_n'])).median():.3f}, P = "
          f"{stats.kruskal(g[f'{band}_mrl'] - 0.89 / np.sqrt(g[f'{band}_n']), m[f'{band}_mrl'] - 0.89 / np.sqrt(m[f'{band}_n'])).pvalue:.2g}")
    gp, mp = g[f"{band}_phase"], m[f"{band}_phase"]
    print(f"Circular mean of preferred phases (0 = peak, degrees): GC {circ_mean_deg(gp):.1f}, MC {circ_mean_deg(mp):.1f}; "
          f"GC minus MC {np.degrees(np.angle(np.exp(1j * (np.angle(np.exp(1j * gp).mean()) - np.angle(np.exp(1j * mp).mean()))))):.1f}")
    print(f"Kruskal-Wallis on phases: (a) on (-pi, pi] P = {stats.kruskal(gp, mp).pvalue:.2g}; "
          f"(b) on [0, 2 pi) P = {stats.kruskal(np.mod(gp, 2 * np.pi), np.mod(mp, 2 * np.pi)).pvalue:.2g}; "
          f"medians (a) GC {np.degrees(gp.median()):.1f}, MC {np.degrees(mp.median()):.1f}; "
          f"(b) GC {np.degrees(np.mod(gp, 2 * np.pi).median()):.1f}, MC {np.degrees(np.mod(mp, 2 * np.pi).median()):.1f}")
    print("By subject, median MRL of modulated units:")
    print(sig.groupby(["subject", "type"])[f"{band}_mrl"].median().unstack().round(3).to_string())
phase_claim("theta")

Result: reproduced. Of the units with Rayleigh P < 0.05 and kappa > 0.1 (483 GC, 532 MC), GC have the higher theta MRL (0.422 against 0.339, Kruskal-Wallis P = 1.5e-20) and fire later in the theta cycle (circular mean 30.8 against 12.0 degrees from the peak; P = 1e-17 with phases on (-pi, pi], P = 0.82 on [0, 2 pi)), so the phase part holds on one of the two readings. GC fire fewer spikes (median 119 against 747), which inflates their MRL; after subtracting the uniform-phase expectation GC are still higher (0.324 against 0.295) but at P = 0.00056, above the paper's 0.0001. In the 17 files where it can be checked, the theta-reference channel sits where DS2 is positive (+459 to +786 uV), below the DS2 reversal; its position in the other files is not known.

gamma-modulation¶

Granule cells are more strongly phase-modulated by gamma oscillations than mossy cells and fire at earlier gamma phases (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for both).

gamma-rate-correlation¶

Slow-firing neurons are more strongly coupled to gamma than fast-firing ones (GC r = -0.176, MC r = -0.184, P < 0.0001 for each).

ds2-recruitment¶

Granule cells are more effectively recruited by type 2 dentate spikes than mossy cells and fire earlier (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for both).

monosyn-gc-to-mc¶

5.5% of granule cells monosynaptically excite mossy cells (32 pairs), whereas no mossy cell significantly excites a granule cell.

Result: partially reproduced. The automatic test of the Methods finds 65 GC to MC pairs and 8 MC to GC pairs among 4713 GC-MC pairs. The GC to MC fraction is 0.107 as pairs over GC, 0.0805 as GC with a target over GC and 0.0138 as pairs over tested pairs, none within 0.0495 to 0.0605, and MC to GC pairs are found, where the paper reports none. GC to MC pairs outnumber MC to GC pairs 65 to 8. The paper inspected each detection by hand and kept 32; that step cannot be repeated. Stricter thresholds lower both counts (56 and 6 at the 99.99999th percentile). For 22 GC to MC pairs the largest bin is the first of the window (1.5 to 2 ms); without them 43 pairs remain (0.0706 of GC). Of the 8 MC to GC pairs, 6 are in YutaMouse33, 4 involve one GC (unit 3 of 150224) that is also synchronous with each of those MC, and 5 are also detected as GC to MC pairs, which fits common input better than an MC to GC connection. In the 17 files that give the shank, 17 of 39 GC to MC pairs are on one shank.

burst-facilitation¶

Spike transmission probability from granule cells to mossy cells increases from the first to the second spike of a granule cell burst (P < 0.001).

In [30]:
rows = []
smap = {s["session"]: s for s in S}
for r in pairs.itertuples():
    s = smap[r.session]
    tg, tm = dg.times(s, r.gc), dg.times(s, r.mc)
    pos = dg.burst_positions(tg)
    rows.append({"single": dg.transmission(tg[pos == 0], tm), "first": dg.transmission(tg[pos == 1], tm),
                 "second": dg.transmission(tg[pos == 2], tm), "third": dg.transmission(tg[pos == 3], tm),
                 "n_first": int((pos == 1).sum()), "n_second": int((pos == 2).sum())})
B = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f"Pairs: {len(B)}; median GC spikes per pair that are first / second in a burst: {B.n_first.median():.0f} / {B.n_second.median():.0f}")
print("Median transmission probability:", B[["single", "first", "second", "third"]].median().round(4).to_dict())
ok = B[["first", "second"]].notna().all(axis=1)
w = stats.wilcoxon(B.second[ok], B.first[ok])
print(f"Second against first: {int((B.second[ok] > B.first[ok]).sum())} of {int(ok.sum())} pairs higher, paired Wilcoxon P = {w.pvalue:.2g}")
for isi in (0.004, 0.010):
    vals = []
    for r in pairs.itertuples():
        s = smap[r.session]; tg, tm = dg.times(s, r.gc), dg.times(s, r.mc); pos = dg.burst_positions(tg, isi)
        vals.append((dg.transmission(tg[pos == 1], tm), dg.transmission(tg[pos == 2], tm)))
    v = np.array(vals); ok2 = np.all(np.isfinite(v), axis=1)
    print(f"Variant, bursts at most {isi * 1000:.0f} ms apart: median first {np.median(v[ok2, 0]):.4f}, second {np.median(v[ok2, 1]):.4f}, P = {stats.wilcoxon(v[ok2, 1], v[ok2, 0]).pvalue:.2g}")
vals = []
for r in pairs.itertuples():
    s = smap[r.session]; tg, tm = dg.times(s, r.gc), dg.times(s, r.mc); pos = dg.burst_positions(tg)
    nxt, prv = np.r_[np.diff(tg), np.inf], np.r_[np.inf, np.diff(tg)]
    first = tg[(pos == 1) & (nxt >= 0.0035)]
    second = tg[(pos == 2) & (prv >= 0.0035)]
    vals.append((dg.transmission(first, tm), dg.transmission(second, tm), dg.transmission(tg[pos == 1], tm, hollow=0.6),
                 dg.transmission(tg[pos == 2], tm, hollow=0.6), dg.transmission(tg[pos == 0], tm, hollow=0.6)))
v = np.array(vals)
ok2 = np.all(np.isfinite(v[:, :2]), axis=1)
print(f"Variant, burst intervals of 3.5 to 6 ms only (no overlap of the two +1.5 to +5 ms windows): median first {np.median(v[ok2, 0]):.4f}, "
      f"second {np.median(v[ok2, 1]):.4f}, second higher in {int((v[ok2, 1] > v[ok2, 0]).sum())} of {int(ok2.sum())}, P = {stats.wilcoxon(v[ok2, 1], v[ok2, 0]).pvalue:.2g}")
ok3 = np.all(np.isfinite(v[:, 2:4]), axis=1)
print(f"Variant, baseline hollowed by 60%: median single {np.nanmedian(v[:, 4]):.4f}, first {np.median(v[ok3, 2]):.4f}, second {np.median(v[ok3, 3]):.4f}, "
      f"P = {stats.wilcoxon(v[ok3, 3], v[ok3, 2]).pvalue:.2g}")
nf = ~first_bin.values
okn = ok & nf
print(f"Variant, without the {int(first_bin.sum())} first-bin pairs: second higher in {int((B.second[okn] > B.first[okn]).sum())} of {int(okn.sum())}, "

Result: reproduced. For the 65 detected pairs, the transmission probability of the second spike of a GC burst (median 0.0334) exceeds that of the first (0.0066) in 58 pairs (paired Wilcoxon P = 1.2e-09), and it holds with bursts defined at 4 ms (P = 4.4e-08) or 10 ms (P = 5.5e-10), with only burst intervals of 3.5 to 6 ms, where the two response windows do not overlap (58 of 65, P = 7.6e-10), with a baseline hollowed by 60% (P = 1.2e-09), and without the 22 first-bin pairs (41 of 43, P = 3.8e-11). The pairs are the automatic detections, more than the paper's 32. First spikes transmit less than single spikes (0.0066 against 0.0147; 0.0067 against 0.0149 with the hollowed baseline), which these outputs do not explain.

state-transmission¶

GC to MC spike transmission is lower during NREM sleep than during waking (n = 31, P < 0.005).

In [31]:
rows = []
for r in pairs.itertuples():
    s = smap[r.session]
    tg, tm = dg.times(s, r.gc), dg.times(s, r.mc)
    out = {}
    for lab in ("awake", "nrem"):
        st = s["states"][s["states"].label == lab]
        keep = np.zeros(len(tg), bool)
        for a, b in zip(st.start_time, st.stop_time):
            keep[np.searchsorted(tg, a):np.searchsorted(tg, b)] = True
        out[lab] = dg.transmission(tg[keep], tm) if keep.sum() >= 50 else np.nan
        out[f"n_{lab}"] = int(keep.sum())
    rows.append(out)
W = pd.DataFrame(rows)
ok = W[["awake", "nrem"]].notna().all(axis=1)
print(f"Pairs with at least 50 GC spikes in both states: {int(ok.sum())} of {len(W)}")
print(f"Median transmission: awake {W.awake[ok].median():.4f}, NREM {W.nrem[ok].median():.4f}; NREM lower in {int((W.nrem[ok] < W.awake[ok]).sum())} pairs; "
      f"paired Wilcoxon P = {stats.wilcoxon(W.nrem[ok], W.awake[ok]).pvalue:.2g}")
okn = ok & ~first_bin.values
print(f"Variant, without the first-bin pairs: median awake {W.awake[okn].median():.4f}, NREM {W.nrem[okn].median():.4f}, NREM lower in "
      f"{int((W.nrem[okn] < W.awake[okn]).sum())} of {int(okn.sum())}, P = {stats.wilcoxon(W.nrem[okn], W.awake[okn]).pvalue:.2g}")
xs = CC[CC.gc_to_mc].in_site_files.values
oks = ok & xs
if oks.sum() >= 5:
    print(f"Variant, pairs in the 17 files with shanks: NREM lower in {int((W.nrem[oks] < W.awake[oks]).sum())} of {int(oks.sum())}, P = {stats.wilcoxon(W.nrem[oks], W.awake[oks]).pvalue:.2g}")

Without the 22 first-bin pairs NREM is lower in 24 of 43 (P = 0.27), and in the 17 files that give the shank in 20 of 39 (P = 0.86).

zero-lag-synchrony¶

Synchronous co-activation within 1 ms is found in 23% of mossy cells and 9% of CA3 pyramidal cells, but in fewer than 0.2% of granule cell pairs.

In [32]:
started = time.time()
rows = []
for s in S:
    ut = s["units"].set_index("unit")
    for ty in ("GC", "MC", "CA3"):
        us = [u for u in s["spikes"] if ut.type[u] == ty]
        T = {u: dg.times(s, u) for u in us}
        for i, a in enumerate(us):
            for b in us[i + 1:]:
                rows.append({"session": s["session"], "type": ty, "a": a, "b": b,
                             "sync": dg.ccg_test(dg.ccg(T[a], T[b]))["sync"], "same_shank_id": ut.shank_id[a] == ut.shank_id[b],
                             "same_group": (eg.get((s["session"], a)) == eg.get((s["session"], b))) if (s["session"], a) in eg.index else np.nan})
Z = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f"Pairs tested in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")
for ty in ("GC", "MC", "CA3"):
    z = Z[Z.type == ty]
    cells = pd.concat([z[["session", "a"]].rename(columns={"a": "u"}), z[["session", "b"]].rename(columns={"b": "u"})]).drop_duplicates()
    synced = pd.concat([z[z.sync][["session", "a"]].rename(columns={"a": "u"}), z[z.sync][["session", "b"]].rename(columns={"b": "u"})]).drop_duplicates()
    print(f"{ty}: (a) pairs {int(z.sync.sum())} of {len(z)} = {z.sync.mean():.4f}; (b) cells with a synchronous partner {len(synced)} of {len(cells)} = {len(synced) / max(1, len(cells)):.4f}")
print("Paper: MC 0.23 (0.207 to 0.253), CA3 0.09 (0.081 to 0.099), GC pairs below 0.002 (up to 0.0022).")
def sync_fracs(z):
    cells = pd.concat([z[["session", "a"]].rename(columns={"a": "u"}), z[["session", "b"]].rename(columns={"b": "u"})]).drop_duplicates()
    synced = pd.concat([z[z.sync][["session", "a"]].rename(columns={"a": "u"}), z[z.sync][["session", "b"]].rename(columns={"b": "u"})]).drop_duplicates()
    return z.sync.mean(), len(synced) / max(1, len(cells)), len(z), len(cells)
print("\nVariant, the 17 files that give each unit's shank:")
Zs = Z[Z.same_group.notna()]
for ty in ("GC", "MC", "CA3"):
    z = Zs[Zs.type == ty]
    a1 = sync_fracs(z); a2 = sync_fracs(z[z.same_group == False])
    print(f"  {ty}: all pairs {a1[0]:.4f} of {a1[2]} pairs, cells {a1[1]:.3f} of {a1[3]}; pairs on different shanks only {a2[0]:.4f} of {a2[2]}, cells {a2[1]:.3f}; "
          f"synchronous pairs on one shank {int(z[z.same_group == True].sync.sum())} of {int(z.sync.sum())}")
def shank_gap(r):
    return abs(int(eg[(r.session, r.a)].replace("shank", "")) - int(eg[(r.session, r.b)].replace("shank", "")))
Zd = Zs[Zs.same_group == False].copy()
Zd["gap"] = [shank_gap(r) for r in Zd.itertuples()]
print("Synchronous pairs by distance between shanks (shank numbers apart; 200 um per step), 17 files:")
print(pd.crosstab(Zd.type, Zd.gap, values=Zd.sync, aggfunc="mean").round(3).to_string())
print(pd.crosstab(Zd[Zd.sync].type, Zd[Zd.sync].gap).to_string())
# One neuron sorted twice would share most of its spikes with its copy; synchrony from common input
# shares a few percent. Coincidence: fraction of the sparser unit's spikes with a partner spike within 0.5 ms.
smap = {s["session"]: s for s in S}
def coincident(s, a, b, tol=0.0005):
    x, y = dg.times(s, a), dg.times(s, b)
    if len(x) > len(y):
        x, y = y, x
    j = np.clip(np.searchsorted(y, x), 1, len(y) - 1)
    return float((np.minimum(np.abs(y[j] - x), np.abs(y[j - 1] - x)) < tol).mean())
Zy = Z[Z.sync].copy()
Zy["coinc"] = [coincident(smap[r.session], r.a, r.b) for r in Zy.itertuples()]
print("\nSynchronous pairs: fraction of the sparser unit's spikes within 0.5 ms of the other's:")
print(Zy.groupby("type").coinc.describe(percentiles=[0.5, 0.9]).round(3).to_string())
print("Pairs above 0.2:", Zy[Zy.coinc > 0.2].groupby("type").size().to_dict())
Zc = Z[~Z.index.isin(Zy[Zy.coinc > 0.2].index)]
for ty in ("MC", "CA3"):
    f = sync_fracs(Zc[Zc.type == ty])
    print(f"Variant without pairs above 0.2, {ty}: pairs {f[0]:.4f}, cells {f[1]:.3f}")

Result: partially reproduced. Synchrony within 1 ms is rare among GC pairs (4 of 3155, 0.0013) and common for MC, but the MC and CA3 values are outside tolerance under both readings: MC 0.0766 of pairs or 0.433 of cells, CA3 0.0120 of pairs or 0.102 of cells, against 0.23 and 0.09. Read as cells, both exceed the GC pair fraction more than ten times. In the 17 files that give the shank, no synchronous pair is on one shank (0 of 160 MC, 0 of 51 CA3), so leaving out same-shank pairs changes the cell fractions little (MC 0.494, CA3 0.267 there). Most synchronous MC pairs are on neighbouring shanks (143 of 160). No synchronous pair shares more than 15% of the sparser unit's spikes within 0.5 ms (MC at most 5.8%), so none looks like one neuron sorted twice.

tmaze-central-active¶

On the circular T-maze, the fraction of active neurons (above 1 Hz) is higher in the central arm than in the side arms, for granule cells, mossy cells and CA3 pyramidal cells (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.00001 for each).

In [33]:
started = time.time()
TMAPS = {}
rows = []
for s in TM:
    ut = s["units"].set_index("unit")
    units = [u for u in s["spikes"] if ut.type[u] in ("GC", "MC", "CA3")]
    if not units:
        continue
    occ, maps, runs = dg.tmaze_maps(s, units)
    TMAPS[s["session"]] = (occ, maps, runs)
    for u in units:
        fields = [(g, f) for g in range(3) for f in dg.linear_fields(maps[u][g])]
        flat = np.concatenate(maps[u])
        rows.append({"session": s["session"], "subject": s["subject"], "unit": u, "type": ut.type[u], "n_fields": len(fields),
                     "field_peak": max([f[2] for _, f in fields], default=np.nan),
                     "info_bits": dg.spatial_info(flat, np.concatenate(occ)), "fields": fields})
F = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f"T-maze maps of {len(F)} units in {len(TMAPS)} sessions, {F.subject.nunique()} mice ({time.time() - started:.0f} s)")
print("Units per type:", F.type.value_counts().to_dict(), "(paper: GC 213, MC 225, CA3 249 in 9 mice)")
for ty in ("GC", "MC", "CA3"):
    stack = [TMAPS[r.session][1][r.unit] for r in F[F.type == ty].itertuples()]
    frac = [np.nanmean(np.array([m[g] for m in stack]) > 1.0, axis=0) for g in range(3)]
    central, side = frac[0], np.concatenate(frac[1:])
    print(f"{ty}: fraction active per bin, central median {np.median(central):.3f} ({len(central)} bins), "
          f"side median {np.median(side):.3f} ({len(side)} bins), Kruskal-Wallis P = {stats.kruskal(central, side).pvalue:.2g}")
print("\nVariant, per unit: fraction of central-arm bins above 1 Hz against fraction of side-arm bins above 1 Hz (Wilcoxon over units):")
for ty in ("GC", "MC", "CA3"):
    cen, sid = [], []
    for r in F[F.type == ty].itertuples():
        m = TMAPS[r.session][1][r.unit]
        cen.append(np.nanmean(m[0] > 1.0)); sid.append(np.nanmean(np.concatenate(m[1:]) > 1.0))
    cen, sid = np.array(cen), np.array(sid)
    d = cen - sid
    print(f"  {ty}: mean central {cen.mean():.3f}, side {sid.mean():.3f}; central higher in {int((d > 0).sum())}, lower in {int((d < 0).sum())} of {len(d)}; "
          f"P = {stats.wilcoxon(cen, sid).pvalue if np.any(d != 0) else np.nan:.2g}")

Result: partially reproduced. The median fraction of active units is higher in the central arm than on the side arms for all three types (GC 0.020 against 0.018, MC 0.314 against 0.272, CA3 0.214 against 0.189), with Kruskal-Wallis P below 0.00001 for MC only (2.2e-06); GC (P = 0.043) and CA3 (P = 0.048) pass at 0.05. The test treats smoothed, neighbouring bins as independent. Compared unit by unit, which avoids this, the central arm is more active for MC (P = 2.8e-05) but not for GC (central higher in 17, lower in 31 of 253 units, P = 0.83) or CA3 (P = 0.21).

Few granule cells have two or more place fields on the T-maze (6.6%), against 57.8% of mossy cells and 36.1% of CA3 pyramidal cells (Kolmogorov-Smirnov P < 0.0001).

tmaze-splitters¶

The fraction of splitter cells, whose central-arm firing predicts the coming turn, is comparable in granule cells, mossy cells and CA3 pyramidal cells.

In [36]:
rows = []
for r in F.itertuples():
    central = [f for g, f in r.fields if g == 0]
    if not central:
        continue
    s = smap[r.session]
    runs = TMAPS[r.session][2]
    split = False
    for a, b, _ in central:
        rates = dg.tmaze_run_rates(s, r.unit, runs, 0, a, b)
        side = np.array([x[2] for x in runs])
        df = pd.DataFrame([{"rate": rates[i, j], "pos": j, "choice": side[i]} for i in range(len(runs)) for j in range(rates.shape[1]) if np.isfinite(rates[i, j])])
        if df.choice.nunique() < 2 or len(df) < 10:
            continue
        p = anova_lm(ols("rate ~ C(pos) + C(choice)", df).fit(), typ=2).loc["C(choice)", "PR(>F)"]
        split |= bool(p < 0.001)
    rows.append({"type": r.type, "splitter": split})
SP = pd.DataFrame(rows)
tab = pd.crosstab(SP.type, SP.splitter)
print("Units with a central-arm field, and splitters among them:")
print(tab.to_string())
print("Fractions:", SP.groupby("type").splitter.mean().round(3).to_dict())
chi = stats.chi2_contingency(tab)
print(f"Chi-square across the three types: chi2 = {chi[0]:.2f}, P = {chi[1]:.2g}")
for a, b in (("GC", "MC"), ("GC", "CA3"), ("MC", "CA3")):
    t2 = tab.loc[[a, b]].reindex(columns=[False, True], fill_value=0)
    print(f"Fisher's exact test {a} against {b}: P = {stats.fisher_exact(t2.values)[1]:.2g}")
print("Expected GC splitters under equal fractions: %.2f" % chi[3][list(tab.index).index("GC")][-1])

Result: reproduced. Splitter cells are rare in every type (0 of 17 GC, 4 of 179 MC and 4 of 141 CA3 with a central-arm field) and their fractions do not differ (chi-square P = 0.76; Fisher's exact test P = 1 for GC against MC and against CA3, 0.73 for MC against CA3). Under equal fractions 0.40 GC splitters would be expected, so the GC comparison has almost no power.

remap-positive¶

For neurons with stable place fields, the remapping index between open fields A and B is above zero in each group (Wilcoxon signed-rank; GC P < 0.05, MC and CA3 P < 0.00001).

    if not units:
        continue
    M = {k: dg.open_field_maps(s, dg.OPEN_FIELDS[k], units, split=True) for k in ("A", "B", "A2")}
    OMAPS[s["session"]] = M
    for u in units:
        r = {"session": s["session"], "subject": s["subject"], "unit": u, "type": ut.type[u]}
        place = False
        for k in ("A", "B", "A2"):
            full, h1, h2 = M[k][u]
            stab = dg.map_corr(h1, h2)
            nf = len(dg.open_field_fields(full))
            r[f"stab_{k}"], r[f"nf_{k}"] = stab, nf
            place |= bool(stab >= 0.5 and nf > 0)
        r["place"] = place
        r["AB"], r["BA2"], r["AA2"] = dg.map_corr(M["A"][u][0], M["B"][u][0]), dg.map_corr(M["B"][u][0], M["A2"][u][0]), dg.map_corr(M["A"][u][0], M["A2"][u][0])
        r["remap"] = r["AA2"] - np.nanmean([r["AB"], r["BA2"]])
        rows.append(r)
OFD = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f"Open-field maps of {len(OFD)} units in {len(OMAPS)} sessions, {OFD.subject.nunique()} mice ({time.time() - started:.0f} s)")
print("Units per type:", OFD.type.value_counts().to_dict(), "(paper: GC 247, MC 181, CA3 317 in 5 mice)")
print("Place cells:", OFD[OFD.place].type.value_counts().to_dict(), "(paper: GC 30, MC 111, CA3 144)")
print("Units without a remapping index (no spikes at speed in a session):", OFD.remap.isna().groupby(OFD.type).sum().to_dict())
P = OFD[OFD.place & OFD.remap.notna()]
for ty in ("GC", "MC", "CA3"):
    x = P[P.type == ty].remap
    print(f"{ty}: place cells {len(x)}, median remapping index {x.median():.3f}, Wilcoxon P = {stats.wilcoxon(x).pvalue:.2g}")
print("\nAll units (variant): " + ", ".join(f"{t} median {OFD[OFD.type == t].remap.median():.3f}" for t in ("GC", "MC", "CA3")))
print("By subject, place cells (n, median index):")
print(P.groupby(["subject", "type"]).remap.agg(["size", "median"]).round(3).unstack().to_string())

remap-gc-lt-mc¶

pv-remap¶

Population-vector remapping is smaller for granule cells than for mossy cells and CA3 pyramidal cells, for populations of 5, 10, 15 and 20 place cells.

Result: reproduced. For populations of 5, 10, 15 and 20 place cells the GC median population-vector remapping index (0.162 to 0.210) is below the MC (0.253 to 0.302) and CA3 (0.251 to 0.352) medians, with Kruskal-Wallis P from 5.8e-35 to 8.1e-190. These P values treat 1000 overlapping draws from the same 27 GC as independent and do not measure the evidence. Single draws overlap: from 71% (5 cells) to 89% (20 cells) of GC draws are below the MC median. With all place cells together the index is 0.22 for GC and 0.25 for MC, and permuting the GC and MC labels gives P = 0.32 for that difference.

inheritance-tmaze¶

Mossy cells rarely inherit place fields from single presynaptic granule cells; of 10 place fields of connected granule cells, only 2 overlapped a field of the postsynaptic mossy cell.

In [41]:

With the partner replaced by a random other MC of the session, the overlap is 0.38 (5th to 95th percentile 0.19 to 0.62), and 33% of draws are at or below 0.31: the overlap with the connected MC is at the chance level, neither above nor below it. The result uses the automatic pair detections.

inheritance-openfield¶

In the open fields, the rate maps of connected granule cells and mossy cells are not correlated within the granule cell's place field (median near 0, n = 19, Wilcoxon P = 0.60).

In the 17 files with the wide-band signal, the DS2 amplitude at the unit's site, read from the wide-band signal, is higher for MC (median +580 uV; fraction positive 1.00) than for GC (median +232 uV, 80% positive; Mann-Whitney P = 2e-40), placing MC deeper below the DS2 reversal, in each of the 4 mice. The site the electrodes table gives disagrees with the wide-band signal (data check); with it the result also holds (MC +271 against GC -38 uV, P = 5.7e-09), but the two sites share the LFP column for 9% of units and the DS2 sign for 63%. The DS2 amplitudes rest on 8 to 365 events per file.

gc-mc-classification¶

K-means clustering on the DS2 amplitude at the unit's site, the NREM to wake rate ratio and two principal components of the waveform's second derivative separates excitatory dentate units into granule cells and mossy cells.

In [44]:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

def d2_features(wave):
    """Second derivative of the waveform normalised to its trough, upsampled to 100 kHz, from the trough
    to 0.8 ms after it; None when the window runs past the waveform's end."""
    tp, at_end, y = dg.trough_to_peak_ms(wave)
    if y is None or not np.isfinite(tp):
        return None, 0
    i = int(np.argmin(y))
    seg = y[i:i + 80]
    short = 80 - len(seg)
    return np.gradient(np.gradient(np.pad(seg, (0, short), mode="edge"))), short

rows = []
for s in SITE:
    ru = s["raw_units"]["units"]
    ty = s["units"].set_index("unit").type
    for u in s["spikes"]:
        if ty[u] not in ("GC", "MC"):
            continue
        r = {"session": s["session"], "unit": u}
        if u in ru and ru[u]["n"] >= 20:
            r["d2_raw"], r["pad_raw"] = d2_features(ru[u]["wave"][None])
        if u in s["waveforms"]:
            r["d2_stored"], r["pad_stored"] = d2_features(s["waveforms"][u])
        rows.append(r)
WF = pd.DataFrame(rows)
K = WF.merge(R[["session", "unit", "type", "subject", "ds2_site_uV", "ds2_rawsite_uV", "rate_nrem", "rate_awake", "rate_awake_home"]], on=["session", "unit"])
n_all = len(K)

def kmeans_agreement(K, feats):
    z = (K[feats].values - K[feats].values.mean(0)) / K[feats].values.std(0)
    lab = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=50, random_state=0).fit_predict(z)
    truth = (K.type == "MC").values.astype(int)
    flip = np.mean(lab == truth) < 0.5
    return max(np.mean(lab == truth), np.mean(lab != truth)), (1 - lab if flip else lab)

def prepare(K, d2col, ds2col, wake_col):
    k = K[K[d2col].notna() & K[ds2col].notna() & (K[wake_col] > 0)].copy()
    pcs = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(np.stack(k[d2col].values))
    k["w_pc1"], k["w_pc2"] = pcs[:, 0], pcs[:, 1]
    k["ratio"] = k.rate_nrem / k[wake_col]
    k["log_ratio"] = np.log10((k.rate_nrem + 1e-3) / k[wake_col])
    k["ds2"] = k[ds2col]
    return k

# Main: wide-band site and unfiltered wide-band waveform, the Methods' NREM / wake ratio with wake as `awake`.
KM = prepare(K, "d2_raw", "ds2_rawsite_uV", "rate_awake")
agree, lab = kmeans_agreement(KM, ["ds2", "ratio", "w_pc1", "w_pc2"])
print(f"GC and MC in the 17 files: {n_all}; used: {len(KM)} (GC {int((KM.type == 'GC').sum())}, MC {int((KM.type == 'MC').sum())}); "
      f"dropped for fewer than 20 spikes in the wide-band window, no DS2 site or a zero awake rate: {n_all - len(KM)}")
print(f"Agreement of the two clusters with the labels: {agree:.3f}")

Result: reproduced. On 364 GC and MC of the 17 files (32 dropped for fewer than 20 spikes in the wide-band window, no DS2 site or a zero awake rate), k-means on the DS2 amplitude at the wide-band site, the NREM to wake rate ratio of the Methods and two components of the second derivative of the unfiltered wide-band waveform agrees with the labels for 95.3% of units (93% to 97% by mouse). Without the DS2 amplitude it is 89.0%, without the first waveform component 88.5%, without the ratio 94.2%. With the log ratio it is 95.6%, with home-cage awake time 94.8%, and with the stored waveforms and the table's site 92.8% (log ratio 94.4%).

Blocked claims¶

gc-mc-distance and gc-backpropagation need the positions of the recording sites in um. The electrodes table gives x, y and z as NaN in every file. The Methods describe 8 sites per shank on the 8-shank probes and 10 on the 6-shank probes, staggered with 20 um vertical separation, but the files do not give the order of the sites in depth, and the table's site numbers do not follow depth: the DS2 profile along them crosses zero more than once on 43 of 64 shanks with a crossing, and a unit's largest wide-band column lies on the shank the table gives for only 45% of units. In the 17 files that give the shank, the data check recovers each shank's columns and the order of its stored waveform channels from the units' spikes, and along that order the DS2 profile crosses zero once on 43 of the 51 shanks that cross (printed below). The order is consistent with depth, which would let these two claims be tested on the 17 files. This attempt wrote no criteria for them and ran no test, so they stay blocked here. In 83 of the 101 files the units do not even say which shank they were recorded on (shank_id is a cluster number, "0-indexed id of cluster of shank").

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's.

  • Units are classified by the dandiset's cell_type labels, not by re-running the paper's classification; the classification is tested separately on the 17 files that give each unit's shank.
  • Interneuron labels mix dentate and CA3 units, which the paper counts apart.
  • The trough-to-peak latency is measured on the stored waveforms (1.6 ms long; their filtering is not stated, and they match the wide-band signal best after a 300 Hz high-pass), where the paper used unfiltered waveforms.
  • Monosynaptic pairs and synchrony are the automatic detections of the Methods' test; the paper inspected and refined each by hand. The claims that use pairs use these detections.
  • Theta and gamma phases come from the file's theta-reference channel in up to an hour of awake periods per file.
  • T-maze runs, the DS2 and light-pulse baselines, the burst definition and the open-field "local maximum" are choices stated in the helper module.
  • Depth is read from the DS2 amplitude at the unit's site, as the files give no site coordinates. The site is the wide-band column where the unit's spike is largest, in the 17 files with the wide-band signal and shanks, as the electrodes table's channel map disagrees with the data.
  • The k-means classification uses the unfiltered wide-band waveform from about 150 s per file.
  • Home-cage awake time, the Methods' wake for the rate ratio, is shown as a variant.

What was found about the dandiset.

  • In 24 files the first unit's spike train is cut short by a multiple of 65,536 spikes, and the missing spikes open the second unit's train; the loader moves them back.
  • The genotypes in the files (6 SST-Cre, 5 Drd2-Cre::Ai35, 4 POMC-Cre::Arch, 1 POMC-Cre::Ai35) do not match the paper's 16 mice (7 SST-Cre, 5 DRD2-Cre::Ai35, 3 POMC-Cre::Ai35, 1 wild type).
  • 83 of 101 files do not say which shank a unit was recorded on, and no file gives site coordinates, so the paper's depth measures can be computed for 17 files only, and distances not at all.
  • The T-maze positions (twhl_linearized, twhl_norm) and the states (quiet, transit) are not described; their meaning is inferred from the values.
  • The dandiset holds 568 MC against the paper's 500, and labels interneurons without their region.
  • The authors' monosynaptic pairs were not converted, so the paper's pair-based results cannot be checked on its own pairs.
  • One file stores 24,286 duplicate light-pulse times, and the files mix two layouts of the units table.
  • In the 17 files with the wide-band signal, the electrodes table's assignment of columns to shanks and sites disagrees with the data: a unit's spike is largest on the shank the table gives for 45% of units, and DS2 profiles along the site numbers are not smooth. The units' shanks and stored waveform channels fit the wide-band signal under one fixed map of columns, the same in all 4 mice, so the error is in the table.
  • The stored waveforms are about 5 times larger than the same spikes in the wide-band signal (gain 5.08, close to 1/0.195, the inverse of the wide-band conversion in uV per count) and match it best after a 300 Hz high-pass; neither the filtering nor the scale is described.
